title: Hermes Agent Consultant: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Why does a written playbook outperform relying on talent alone?
options: It removes the need to verify work before it ships
It lets the same quality ship regardless of how tired or distracted the consultant is
It guarantees every project will be identical in its details
It eliminates the need to run a retrospective after each engagement
questions.explanation: A written playbook carries the process so quality does not depend on the consultant being sharp or rested, which instinct alone cannot sustain across many engagements.

questions.question: What should you recommend when a task follows a fixed, deterministic procedure?
options: A script, which is faster and never invents output
An agent, because autonomous systems always beat scripts
An agent with a human reviewing every single step
A larger agent with more tools to cover the fixed procedure
questions.explanation: A fixed, deterministic task is better served by a script, which is faster, cheaper, and never invents output.

questions.question: Which form of expansion best keeps a client relationship alive?
options: A single larger one-off project
A hard sell at the moment of handover
Cold outreach to replace clients who go quiet
A standing deliverable on a schedule that keeps running for the client
questions.explanation: A standing deliverable keeps the account in a paying relationship and is easier to say yes to than a bigger one-off, which ends and lets the relationship go silent.

questions.question: An agent reports that it updated a record. What does this statement represent?
options: A claim, which is not proof until the record itself is read back and checked
A verified result, because the agent says it completed the task it described
A repeatable gate, because the same update could be applied again later on
A tool trace, because the agent has named the specific action it performed
questions.explanation: What the agent says is a claim, and only reading the result back in the system turns that claim into evidence.

questions.question: What is the orchestrator's role in a portfolio of agent work?
options: To personally finish the most important card so that it is certain to ship correctly
To decompose the goal, assign each card, and step back from doing the work
To watch every worker closely and correct its output while the work is produced
To reassign each card to a new worker at every stage to build in redundancy
questions.explanation: An orchestrator scales by turning a goal into cards, assigning each to the right worker, and stepping back rather than becoming the bottleneck.

questions.question: When is a whole-gateway restart the right repair?
options: When a job fails on every run because its provider key is invalid
When a skill is misconfigured and fails whenever it loads
When the agent is looping or holds a poisoned connection
When a scheduled job's configuration cannot succeed at startup
questions.explanation: A restart clears live-process state, so it fits a stuck loop or poisoned connection; against a persistent misconfiguration it just repeats the same failure with less evidence.

questions.question: Which task is ready to become a recurring scheduled job?
options: One that worked once but needed your judgment at several points
One you are confident will behave the same way next week without testing
One that produced a reliable result when you ran it by hand
One that is barely stitched together but saves time if it works
questions.explanation: You automate a win that already works reliably by hand; scheduling something unproven just automates a failure on a fixed timetable.

questions.question: What mainly separates an agent-implementation consultant from a builder?
options: The consultant keeps sole ownership and maintains the agent forever
The consultant designs to personal taste instead of a contract
The consultant implements for a client and hands it over
The consultant builds only for their own product and its users
questions.explanation: A builder makes agents for themselves or a product; a consultant implements for a client and must leave that client able to run the system without them.

questions.question: Why deploy a separate profile for each engagement?
options: To make the agent respond faster on each machine
To share one set of credentials across every client
To reduce the number of installs you perform
To stop one client's state bleeding into another's
questions.explanation: A separate home per engagement keeps one client's prompts, memory, credentials, and state from contaminating another client's agent.

questions.question: How should a large goal be decomposed into tasks?
options: Slice by activity, such as writing the tests first and then the code and the docs
Slice by convenience, doing the easiest work first so that momentum builds early
Slice by file, giving one separate task to every file that the change will touch
Slice by deliverable, test each slice against the window, and order by risk
questions.explanation: Splitting by what you produce rather than what you are doing gives slices a client could accept, and risk-first ordering makes a surprise cheap.

questions.question: What makes a change diagnostic instead of a gamble?
options: You change several variables at once so the symptom clears sooner
You change one variable, verify it, and keep a rollback ready
You change only the provider model and never the configuration
You restart the process before making any configuration change
questions.explanation: One change and one check at a time means that when the fix works you know the single cause, and a checkpoint makes each step reversible.

questions.question: What is the difference between a plan and an artifact?
options: A plan is the deliverable the client pays for, and an artifact is optional supporting detail
A plan runs against the live system, and an artifact describes what the plan will do
A plan describes work someone intends to do, and an artifact is the work itself
A plan is verified by a checklist, and an artifact is verified by a human reviewer
questions.explanation: Clients pay for the working result they can run or verify, while a description of intended work is only a plan dressed up as delivery.

questions.question: What is the first move when diagnosing a live failure?
options: Restart the gateway to clear the failure state
Change the most likely configuration key and observe the effect
Tell the client the fix is complete to stop the questions
Preserve the evidence before changing the system
questions.explanation: The first action taken to fix a problem often destroys the evidence needed to understand it, so you secure the record before touching anything.

questions.question: Why must a reviewer be someone other than the builder?
options: Because reviewing takes time the builder cannot spare on delivery
Because shared context produces shared blind spots in the work
Because the reviewer is usually more senior than the builder
Because a second pass by the same author takes longer to complete
questions.explanation: Builder blindness is universal: a reviewer who shares the builder's session, memory, and assumptions reads the artifact the same way and misses the same gap.

questions.question: What makes a capability real, rather than merely claimed?
options: The agent giving a clear and confident description of the work it believes it performed
Evidence it actually fired, such as a tool call, an artifact, or output you can inspect
The capability appearing in the software's published list of features and supported tools
The agent confirming that it has completed the task and reporting the result as done
questions.explanation: A capability is real only when it leaves evidence of having fired; a confident summary is not proof that a tool ran.

questions.question: Why does a shared standard such as MCP matter for wiring an agent into external systems?
options: It removes the need for any credentials when an agent reaches a hosted external system
It replaces many one-off connectors with a single agreed way to expose and reach external tools
It guarantees that every external system exposes exactly the same fixed set of actions to any agent
It lets an agent operate without a model by executing the remote server's own internal code
questions.explanation: A shared protocol lets an agent reach many external systems through configuration rather than bespoke code that breaks when a vendor changes its API.

questions.question: Why is an execution history alone not enough for observability?
options: It records too little detail about which model ran the job
It cannot tell you when a scheduled job last fired
It proves the work ran, not that the output was right
It disappears whenever the gateway restarts unexpectedly
questions.explanation: Observability has two floors; execution history covers only the first, and correctness requires sampling the substance of the output.

questions.question: What belongs in the body of a skill?
options: An ordered procedure with its pitfalls and checks
A narrative of the incident with dates and ticket numbers
A transcript of how the tool first failed during discovery
A list of every client the procedure has been used for
questions.explanation: Skills hold rules rather than logs: a general rule plus a short why, attached to the step it affects and stated once.

questions.question: Why is building before scoping a trap in a consulting engagement?
options: It is faster and lowers the client's total cost
The client is not obliged to pay for work that was never agreed
Scope grows on its own once the agent is running
A working demo removes the need for a written definition of done
questions.explanation: Without an agreed scope the client never committed to what you built, so it is under no obligation to pay for your guess.

questions.question: What should a retrospective after an engagement produce?
options: A full rewrite of the framework every time
Nothing, since the framework is set once and applied unchanged
One or two targeted changes that update the framework
A record of the client's personality for future negotiations
questions.explanation: A retrospective is meant to yield a few targeted improvements, which keeps the framework a living tool that gets sharper instead of a stale document people stop trusting.

questions.question: Why does the lifecycle place support after handover instead of treating go-live as the finish?
options: Support exists mainly to extend the contract for more revenue
The client most needs you as the design meets reality
Handover cannot begin until the support window has closed
Support removes the need for a validation record
questions.explanation: Production is where the design meets the real world, so the client needs support most in the first weeks after go-live.

questions.question: What must happen before you add the gateway, cron, or skills?
options: Prove a clean conversation works before layering
Connect every platform the client might ever use
Turn on cron and skills so the system is complete
Install the desktop app alongside the command line
questions.explanation: Each feature you add is a variable, so the base conversation must be proven before any layer is trusted.

questions.question: When is an agent the right tool for a task?
options: When the client is excited about AI and will pay for it
When the work is judgment-shaped, bounded, and high-volume
When no human is available to review the output
When the task is a fixed rule applied to predictable inputs
questions.explanation: An agent earns its cost on work that needs judgment, stays inside reviewable bounds, and repeats often enough to repay the build.

questions.question: Why must least privilege be enforced by guardrails rather than by the agent behaving carefully?
options: Because a careful agent runs faster than one that has to ask permission for each action
Because a guardrail refuses on its own when care fails, as with a hostile input
Because guardrails make the agent's own output more accurate and more complete
Because a client cannot observe what the agent does without enforced limits in place
questions.explanation: Guardrails are mechanisms that refuse; they hold when the agent is careless or a hostile input steers it, which is exactly when carefulness fails.

questions.question: Which condition marks the end of the design phase in an engagement?
options: The client has signed off on what will be built
The agent has been built and validated on real cases
The problem has been stated in a single agreed sentence
The support window has closed cleanly
questions.explanation: The design phase ends only when the client has approved, in writing, what will be built and where its boundaries lie.

questions.question: Which kind of work belongs in script mode, running no model at all?
options: Client-facing prose where a weaker answer costs more than the tokens saved
Mechanical jobs fully determined by a script, such as threshold checks
Deciding what a report means when the reasoning is non-trivial
Handling a tricky intake reply that needs judgment
questions.explanation: Mechanical jobs belong in script mode, where they cost nothing and cannot drift; putting them on an agent is a common, invisible overspend.

questions.question: When is the right moment to raise the next engagement with a client?
options: At the end of the contract, once the work has faded into routine
Only when the client brings it up first
At the moment the delivered work proves its value while the benefit is fresh
Before delivering anything, so the client commits early
questions.explanation: Clients expand a relationship when they feel its value most sharply, so the ask belongs at the point of proven value rather than after the benefit has faded into routine.

questions.question: Why must a scheduled job's instructions be self-contained?
options: Because every run starts in a fresh session that inherits none of your context
Because the scheduler rejects a prompt that names more than one external system
Because the model forgets the names of its tools between separate executions of a job
Because unattended runs are forbidden from calling any tool that needs a credential
questions.explanation: A scheduled run is a fresh session with none of your memory, so the prompt must carry the target, the action, and the output shape on its own.

questions.question: When is a fixed-fee price the right model for an engagement?
options: When the outcome is well defined and the work is familiar
When the scope is still unknown and the work is exploratory
When the client needs ongoing monitoring and incident response
When the client will not sign any written agreement
questions.explanation: Fixed-fee pricing works when the outcome is defined tightly and familiar enough that you can absorb the overrun; work whose scope is unknown or shifting belongs under a model that moves that uncertainty to the client.

questions.question: When a problem arises mid-engagement, which four things should a well-formed update name?
options: The fix, the timeline, the cost, and the owner
The client, the budget, the deadline, and the apology
The observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target
The date discovered, the date reported, the date resolved, and the date billed
questions.explanation: Naming the observed failure, the investigation, the blast radius, and the verification target turns a vague worry into a bounded, owned problem the client can plan around.

questions.question: What does it mean to verify before you claim in a status update?
options: Report from memory of the plan rather than from the record
Pair every assertive word with its proof, checking the claim against the real state of the work
Send the most confident version first and correct it later if challenged
Only verify once, at the very end of the engagement before handover
questions.explanation: A claim reflects reality only when the reality supports it, so each assertive word is backed by checking the live system, log, or record before the update goes out.

questions.question: Which ROI mistake most damages a consultant's credibility?
options: Quoting a range so wide it covers every outcome
Naming the success metric after the deal instead of before it
Pricing from the numbers gathered during discovery
Claiming the agent replaces the whole job
questions.explanation: An ROI case collapses when it claims more than the agent actually changes; claim only the routine slice and count human review as a cost.

questions.question: What is the real decision a pricing model makes for a piece of consulting work?
options: How many hours the work will ultimately consume
How much profit margin to build into the rate
Which side bears the risk that the scope turns out different than expected
Which invoicing schedule the client prefers
questions.explanation: An engagement model is a contract about which side carries the risk that the scope turns out bigger or different than expected; that risk split, not the rate, is the real decision.

questions.question: What separates a completed handover from a system that is merely finished and delivered?
options: A named client team member owns it going forward
A complete record of every build step is written into a wiki
A final walkthrough is presented to the client's stakeholders
The system has passed one last round of acceptance testing
questions.explanation: Handover is the transfer of ownership, so it is complete when a real person on the client's team is accountable for running and changing the system.

questions.question: Why should a skill's description name the situation it applies to rather than just its topic?
options: It is displayed to the client as the title of the deliverable
It is the only part loaded when relevance is decided
It determines which model tier the skill's work runs on
It stores the credentials the skill needs at run time
questions.explanation: Only the description is loaded at the moment relevance is decided, so naming the situation earns the skill a chance to load.

questions.question: What is a quiet failure?
options: A job that runs and delivers cleanly but whose output is wrong
A job that fails to run and raises an alert immediately
A job that is blocked at startup for a misconfiguration
A job whose delivery reaches the wrong destination and is flagged
questions.explanation: A quiet failure trips no status check because status checks look at whether work completed, not whether it was correct, so the client often finds it first.

questions.question: If you never verify which settings the running agent honors, why is 'it works on my machine' a problem?
options: The agent may work only because of settings absent elsewhere
The install always rewrites the config file it reads
A running agent ignores the config file entirely
Secrets in the environment are always overridden by defaults
questions.explanation: Configuration is resolved through layers that can override your file, so only the behavior the running agent shows is real evidence.

questions.question: What is the fix for a scope that lists inclusions but excludes nothing?
options: Adding inclusions until the client stops asking for more
Writing exclusions plainly, since they stop scope creep
Lowering the price so new requests feel expensive
Waiting for the client to withdraw their requests
questions.explanation: A scope with only inclusions cannot stop scope creep, because every new request appears to be part of the problem; written exclusions are what keep the work on time and on budget.

questions.question: What does a user most need in order to trust an agent that is not always right?
options: A guarantee that it will never be wrong
Clear confidence signals and a fast way to correct it
A mandate from management that everyone must use it anyway
Full control over its architecture and deployment
questions.explanation: Users cannot plan around invisible failure, so clear confidence signals and a fast way to correct the agent are what build trust.

questions.question: What makes the approvers and the users different audiences to design for?
options: Approvers can block it; users decide if it survives
Approvers use the tool every day; users only sign the paperwork
Approvers care about speed; users care only about compliance
Approvers and users are usually the same people with the same concern
questions.explanation: Approvers can block the deployment outright, while users decide through daily use whether it succeeds or quietly fails.

questions.question: What is the actual job of a written scope or statement of work?
options: To satisfy a legal requirement and shift blame onto the client
To replace a fragile shared memory of a verbal agreement with something both sides can inspect
To lock the price so it can never change under any circumstances
To list the deliverables while leaving the exclusions unstated
questions.explanation: A written scope replaces an unreliable shared memory of the conversation with a record both sides can inspect, so neither can drift from the agreement quietly.

questions.question: An integration is configured and the server connects. What is still needed before the connection can be claimed to a client?
options: A real task run against the live system, watched end to end
A note in the handover describing how each server was configured
Confirmation from the server that its processes started without error
A successful connection test showing the endpoint is reachable
questions.explanation: Configuring a server is not the same as it succeeding against the live system, so a real task is watched fire end to end before the integration is claimed.

questions.question: What distinguishes a guardrail from a policy rule?
options: A guardrail is written in more precise legal language than a rule
A guardrail is reviewed by the client while a rule is written by the agent
A guardrail is optional while a rule is mandatory
A guardrail is enforced by the platform regardless of the agent
questions.explanation: A guardrail does not rely on the agent choosing to behave; it mechanically refuses, which is what makes it hold under unattended operation.

questions.question: What is the difference between status and progress in client communication?
options: Status is where the work actually is now, while progress is the distance traveled toward done
Status is how you feel about the work, while progress is what the client asks about
Status and progress mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably
Status is the billing total, while progress is the remaining budget
questions.explanation: Status is a fact about where the work is right now against the plan, while progress is how far you have moved toward done; keeping them separate stops you from reporting progress while a blocker hides a stall.

questions.question: What is the difference between an agent's tools and its skills?
options: Tools are the actions an agent can take, and skills are the procedures it follows
Tools are the procedures an agent follows, and skills are the actions it can take
Tools are the credentials an agent stores, and skills are the toolsets it turns on
Tools are the on-demand documents an agent loads, and skills are the commands it may run
questions.explanation: Tools are the verbs an agent can execute, while skills carry the procedures that make it act the client's way, and the two fail differently when missing.

questions.question: A scheduled job completed and produced its report, but no one received it. What is the correct reading?
options: The job succeeded, because a completed run always reaches its recipient
The failure is unrelated to the schedule and can be ignored
The report should be regenerated by hand and sent again
This is a delivery failure, which fails separately from the run itself
questions.explanation: Run failure and delivery failure are tracked separately, so a job whose output reaches nobody has not delivered anything even though it ran.

questions.question: What distinguishes decision review from artifact review?
options: Artifact review requires a human while decision review can be scripted
Artifact review is done by the builder while decision review is done by the client
Artifact review happens after delivery while decision review happens before
Artifact review checks output while decision review judges approach
questions.explanation: Artifact review is mechanical and should be automated; decision review asks whether the approach was right and is where a human reviewer earns their place.

questions.question: What does each approver need in order to say yes?
options: The same demo and price shown to all of them
One combined sign-off covering value, risk, and operations
A distinct artifact tied to what that approver owns
Proof the agent is cheaper than every alternative
questions.explanation: Owners approve value, IT approves operations, and compliance approves risk, so each one needs an artifact aimed at what they own.

questions.question: What makes a deployment a real delivery rather than a prototype?
options: The agent works once during a demo on the consultant's laptop
The code and the data directory are stored on the same disk
The agent runs always-on in the client's own channel
The installer finished without reporting any errors
questions.explanation: A laptop terminal is a prototype; a delivery runs always-on and is reachable in the channel the client's team already uses.

questions.question: Where should a card's acceptance criteria live, and why?
options: In a shared document that the worker is instructed to open before it begins the task
In the orchestrator's private memory, which the worker can query whenever it needs to
In the assignee's prior handoffs from similar tasks it has completed before
On the card itself, because the worker reads only the card and its own thread
questions.explanation: The worker reads only the card and its thread, so the definition of done must sit on the card in verifiable terms or no one can check it.

questions.question: How should a reviewer reject a candidate?
options: Route it back to the implementer with a reason
Block the card so the blocked column records the rejection
Leave a comment and let the implementer decide whether to act
Reopen the task in triage so a new scope is written
questions.explanation: A verdict is a routable decision: rejection returns the work to the implementer with a reason, while block is reserved for real escalation, since using it for rejection burns the signal.

questions.question: Where does the most reliable picture of the real problem come from?
options: The executive who signs the contract and owns the budget
The compliance officer who sets the rules
The consultant's own experience with similar clients
The people who perform the task, watched doing the work
questions.explanation: The people who do the task day to day know where it actually breaks, and they speak more frankly than the sponsor who is selling the project.

questions.question: What makes a piece of data a secret?
options: Its length and the mix of unusual characters that appear inside it
Whether it is stored inside a file that ends in the env extension
The fact that the client specifically asked you to keep the value private
The access it unlocks, no matter how short or unremarkable it looks
questions.explanation: A secret is defined by the access it unlocks, not by its appearance, so a short token that reaches customer records is treated with full care.

questions.question: How should a fleet check be run?
options: Only when the client reports that something looks wrong
On a schedule so it fires without you being asked
Whenever you happen to remember to open the dashboard
Once at the end of the engagement as part of the handover
questions.explanation: If the check depends on remembering to look or on the client reporting a problem, it is a support ticket rather than observability; schedule it so it runs whether or not anyone asks.

questions.question: Why does a small task ship more reliably than a large one?
options: Because a small task does not need to be verified once it has been finished
Because a small task can safely be handed to a less experienced worker
Because the whole result fits in view, so it can be finished and verified
Because a large task is always more valuable and therefore justifies the extra effort
questions.explanation: A task small enough to see whole can be finished and verified, which is what lets you truthfully report it as done.

questions.question: What is the correct default for dangerous commands in unattended scheduled work?
options: Approve them automatically so that the recurring job never stalls partway through
Let the agent decide for itself whether each individual command is safe to run
Deny them, so the job must find a safe path or fail in a way that is visible
Approve them only after the job has already run successfully several times
questions.explanation: Unattended work defaults to denying dangerous commands, because a failure you can see is safer than a destructive command that no one approved.

questions.question: When turning a measured unit cost into client pricing, what should drive the number?
options: Your labor, with inference budgeted and both put in writing
The inference bill, since that is what varies month to month
The number of features delivered in the current release
The competitor's published per-seat subscription rate
questions.explanation: Inference is a small part of the cost while your labor is the large one, so you price your labor, budget the inference, and state both plus a ceiling.

questions.question: What are the parts of a good refusal to build an agent?
options: Name the reason, the needed change, and an alternative
Decline politely and end the relationship without explanation
Accept the project and quietly reduce its scope later
Blame the client's data and withdraw from the engagement
questions.explanation: A good refusal is not a dead end: it states the reason, names what would make the agent right, and offers what works today.

questions.question: What does the discovery and scoping phase produce?
options: A written scope and an honest go or no-go call
A trained client team and the handed-over keys
A validation record of real cases and safe failures
A running agent in production with monitoring in place
questions.explanation: Discovery and scoping end in a written scope and an honest decision about whether an agent is the right answer, before any building starts.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the finishing discipline?
options: Saying it should work is an acceptable status whenever the design itself looks sound
A run that completed is the same thing as a verified and working final result
Capturing what the work taught you is an optional step once the task is delivered
A claim is finished only when verified, and the reusable part is captured
questions.explanation: Verification is the finish line, and capturing the reusable part lets the next piece of work start further along than the last one did.
